transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, honestly, I'm here because things have just been... really off lately, and it's starting to affect my day-to-day. You see, I work in healthcare support, so I'm on my feet constantly, moving patients, running around, and usually I need a solid meal to keep me going. But lately, my eating has just gotten so completely out of whack. I mean, there are some days where I wake up, and the very thought of food is just... it's like I can't even process it. I'll barely manage to force down a cup of coffee and maybe half a granola bar before I have to clock in for a shift. And it's not just a one-off thing, it's been happening so much that I've actually started noticing it in my clothes. My scrubs, the ones I wear every single day, they've been hanging loose on me, bagging around the waist and shoulders. And the thing is, I'm not trying to lose weight at all. I haven't changed my routine, I'm not dieting, I'm just... not eating because the drive to eat is just gone. It's concerning, you know, because I need my strength for work, but I just can't seem to make myself eat a normal meal anymore.
Have you been trying to lose weight?

No, no, not at all. That's the thing, I haven't been trying to lose weight in the slightest. Like I was saying, my eating has just gotten so completely off track lately. It's like my appetite just packed up and left. Some days, I wake up and the thought of breakfast is just... it's too much. I'll barely get down a cup of coffee and maybe a granola bar before I have to head in for a long shift at the hospital. And you know, working in healthcare support, I need my energy. I'm lifting, I'm moving, I'm constantly on the go. I should be starving by lunchtime, but I'm just not. And because of all this, I've really noticed it in my clothes. My scrubs, which used to fit perfectly fine, they're just hanging loose on me now. They bag around my waist, they slide off my shoulders... it's really frustrating because I'm absolutely not trying to diet or anything like that. I just have zero desire to eat, and the weight is just falling off me without me doing a single thing to make it happen.
Are you happy about the weight loss?

Happy? No, God, no. I mean, I know some people would be thrilled to drop a few pounds without hitting the gym or whatever, but for me, it's... well, like I said, it's literally what brings me in to see you today. It's really distressing. My eating has just gotten so incredibly off, and it's not a good feeling at all. 

When I wake up and I have to stare down that cup of coffee and that same dry granola bar—which, like I was telling you, is sometimes the absolute maximum I can get down before a shift—I just feel this... this frustration. I have to force myself to chew it, and it tastes like sawdust. I have to wash it down with the coffee just to swallow. And then I get dressed for work, and I put on my scrubs, and like I mentioned, they're just hanging so loose on me now. I have to yank the drawstrings so tight just to keep the pants from sliding down while I'm trying to transfer a patient from a bed to a wheelchair. It's honestly embarrassing to be constantly adjusting my uniform all day in front of my coworkers because my body is just shrinking. 

I'm 46 years old, I need my muscle, I need my stamina for this job, you know? It's physical work. So no, I'm definitely not happy about it. I'm just worried, because I'm absolutely not trying to lose weight, and my appetite is just... it's just completely broken, and I don't know how to fix it.
Have you been feeling anxious or stressed about anything in particular lately?

Well, anxious... yes, I suppose you could say that, but it's not just regular stress like paying the bills or, you know, normal work stuff. It's... it's very specific, and it's been eating at me constantly. It's at the clinic where I work. I mean, we've had this new workflow system rolled out recently, right? And everyone says it's just standard procedure, just a way to streamline things. But I've been noticing things that don't add up. 

I keep getting stuck on this idea, this... this feeling, really, that certain people there—specifically a couple of the nurses and one of the shift coordinators—are watching me. Not just watching, but actively monitoring my charting times. Like, every time I log in to update a patient's chart after a transfer or after taking vitals, I feel this intense scrutiny. And it's not just a feeling, I see it in the schedule. They leave these little signs, these subtle changes in the shift rotations and the break times, and they always seem to align perfectly with when I'm supposed to be on the floor. It's like they're trying to catch me slipping up, trying to build a case against me to get me fired. 

I've even brought it up to my supervisor. I went into her office last Tuesday, closed the door, and laid it all out for her. I showed her the schedule, pointed out the patterns, the way my name is always grouped with the heaviest patient loads right when the coordinator is at the main desk. And she just looked at me and said, "It's just the new workflow, it's random, everyone is adjusting." But it doesn't feel random. It feels deliberate. It feels like they're communicating through the system, sending messages to each other about me. And no matter how much my supervisor tries to brush it off as just the new software or whatever, I can't shake it. It's exhausting, honestly, going into work every day feeling like you're walking into a trap that they're slowly pulling tight around you. So yeah, I guess that's making me pretty anxious.
Do you think anyone else would notice this monitoring if they looked at the schedules and charts?

Well, you see, that's the thing. That's exactly what I tried to explain to my supervisor when I went into her office. I mean, I brought the printed schedules right in there with me. I highlighted the sections. I said, "Look, look right here at how the shift coordinator's desk time perfectly overlaps with my heaviest charting periods on the east wing." And she just... she didn't see it. Or she pretended not to see it, I don't know. 

She just kept repeating the same company line, you know? "It's just the new workflow, everyone's schedule is a little chaotic right now, it's just the algorithm." The algorithm! Like a computer program just accidentally decides to put a target on my back. But I know what I'm seeing. I keep getting stuck on this idea, this absolute certainty, that they are watching my charting times specifically. And these little signs in the schedule... they aren't just typos or random computer glitches. They are deliberate markers. It's like a code they're using to show each other that they're building a case against me. 

But to answer your question, no, I don't think anyone else would notice it just by glancing at it. Because they aren't the ones being targeted. When you're the one in the crosshairs, when it's your livelihood on the line, you notice the patterns. You see the subtle shifts in the break times, the way the nurses suddenly congregate near the terminal when I log in. A regular person, another tech or a doctor walking by, they'd just see a busy clinic. They'd just see the "new workflow" functioning like it's supposed to. They wouldn't see the trap. But I see it. I see it every single day, no matter how much my supervisor tries to tell me it's all in my head or just a scheduling quirk. It's not a quirk. It's a case being built, brick by brick, right there in the charting logs.
Do you think it's possible that your interpretation of the scheduling patterns might be incorrect?

Incorrect? I mean... I guess anything is technically possible, right? If you want to get philosophical about it, maybe I'm misinterpreting gravity when an apple falls from a tree. But... no. No, I don't think I'm incorrect. I really don't. Because, like I keep saying, I keep getting stuck on this idea—this reality, really—that certain people at the clinic are watching my charting times. 

It's not just a passing thought, doctor. It's not like I had a bad day and thought, "Oh, they're out to get me." It's an everyday thing. I go in, I look at the schedule, and there they are—these little signs in the schedule. And I know my supervisor tells me it's just the new workflow, she tells me it's just the algorithm adjusting to the patient load, but she's not the one logging in at 2:15 PM and seeing three different nurses suddenly check the same system right when I'm entering my vitals for room 4. She's not seeing the way my lunch break gets pushed back exactly on the days when the shift coordinator is doing her weekly audits. 

It's too specific. It's too perfectly aligned to be a mistake or a coincidence. They are leaving these signs to show they're building a case against me. It's like they want me to know, in this subtle, deniable way, that they have the upper hand. So when my supervisor sits there and tells me it's just the workflow... it just feels like she's either incredibly naive or she's part of it, too. I don't want to think she's part of it, because she's always been fair to me in the past, but how can she not see it? How can anyone look at those schedules, look at the charting times, and tell me I'm incorrect? I'm the one living it. I'm the one whose job is on the line. So no, I don't think I'm misinterpreting it at all. It's happening, and it's exhausting trying to pretend it's not.
Have you always felt like you're being monitored at work, or is this a relatively new feeling?

Well, no, not always. I mean, I've been working in healthcare support for a long time, and I never used to have these issues. I used to just go in, do my shift, take the vitals, help the patients, and go home. It was fine. Completely normal. I actually really liked my job back then. But then... well, they did this whole massive overhaul with the shift changes at the clinic. This was a while back. And at first, it was just chaotic, like any administrative change, you know how it is, everyone complaining about their new hours. 

But then, a few months after those shift changes happened... that's when things shifted for me. So, if I'm doing the math right, looking back at the calendar, it was about a year and eight months ago that all this really started. That's exactly when I started getting that sense that people were sending signs through the schedule. It definitely wasn't there before. 

And... well, honestly, it wasn't just the schedule either. That's also when the voices started. I don't think I mentioned that to you yet, but yeah, about a year and eight months ago, right when the schedule stuff started becoming so obvious to me, I started hearing them. Just these voices, you know, whispering about my charting, commenting on how I was doing things, saying I was going to get caught. It all started at the exact same time, just a few months after they changed the shifts around. 

So it's not like I've felt this way my whole life, or even my whole career. It's very specifically tied to that time period. Before that, everything was fine, I was just a regular tech doing my job. But since that point, a year and eight months ago, it's just been this relentless... this constant pressure. The voices, the signs in the schedule, the way they all overlap and coordinate with each other. I mean, you try dealing with that for almost two years and see if you don't feel completely drained by it. It's not a new feeling anymore because I've been living in it for so long now, but it definitely has a very specific starting point. It's just... it's a lot to carry every single shift.
Are the voices you hear audible to you, or are they more like thoughts in your head?

Oh, no, they are definitely audible. It's not... it's not like my own internal monologue, you know? It's not me just having a bad thought about myself or worrying about my performance. It's real, physical sound. It’s outside of me. 

Like, I'll be walking down the hallway, right? Just doing my normal rounds, maybe carrying some charts or taking some samples down to the lab. And I'll hear it clear as day. I'll hear my name. Just someone saying my name right behind me. Or, a lot of times, I'll be near the phlebotomy room—you know, that little room right past the double doors on the second floor where we do the blood draws—and I'll just be in there prepping the vials, making sure the labels are right, because you really can't afford to make mistakes with the labels, and I'll hear these short comments. It's usually something really specific, like someone will just say, "he messed up again." 

And I'll spin around immediately, because I think it's my supervisor or one of the floor nurses trying to catch me making a mistake, or maybe someone from the algorithm team checking up on me. But... I look, and there is absolutely nobody there. The hallway is completely empty. The phlebotomy room is empty. It's just me and the hum of the fluorescent lights and the blood centrifuge. But the voice is so real, doctor, it echoes off the linoleum, you know what I mean? A thought doesn't have an acoustic bounce to it. A thought doesn't make you physically turn your head. 

And the strangest part about it, the thing that really gets me, is that I've tried to track when it happens. I thought, well, maybe I'm just stressed or feeling really down, because I do get really down sometimes, like this heavy, heavy fog just sits on me and I can barely get out of bed. But I've noticed it doesn't even matter how I'm feeling. It can happen even on days when I’m not especially sad. I could be having a perfectly fine morning, drinking my coffee, feeling totally okay about the shift, and then bam—"he messed up again"—right in my ear when the room is completely empty. It just catches me off guard every single time because it sounds exactly like a physical person standing two feet behind me, breathing the same air. So no, it's not a thought. It's an actual voice.
Do you think the voices or the feeling of being monitored have anything to do with your lack of appetite?

My appetite? I... well, I don't know. I haven't really sat down and tried to connect those dots, to be perfectly honest with you. I mean, I guess it’s a fair question, because everything kind of bleeds together when you're under this much stress, but... I don't really see a direct link there. 

It is true that I haven't been eating much, though. Like, just yesterday, I brought this turkey and swiss sandwich on rye—I usually get the rye bread from this little bakery down on 4th street because it doesn't get soggy in the breakroom fridge—but I just left it sitting in my locker the entire shift. I walked into the breakroom around 1:00 PM, and someone was heating up leftover fish in the microwave, which is just terrible breakroom etiquette to begin with, but my stomach just immediately tied itself into a tight little knot. I just looked at the fridge and thought, I can't do it. I can't eat. 

But is that because I'm worried about the schedule algorithms or the voices? I really couldn't tell you. I mean, sure, when you're constantly looking over your shoulder in the phlebotomy room, or when you're checking the charting times to see who is logging in at the exact same second as you, you aren't exactly working up a big appetite. Your body is just tense all the time. You're on edge. But honestly, even on my days off, when I'm at home and I'm miles away from the clinic, and the schedule isn't right in front of my face... I still just look at a plate of food and feel absolutely nothing. It's like chewing cardboard. It just feels like so much physical effort just to chew and swallow. 

Especially when that heavy fog rolls in, like I was telling you about earlier. When I get in those moods where just pulling the blankets off and getting out of bed feels like trying to walk through wet cement... eating is the absolute last thing on my mind. I'll go a whole weekend and realize on Sunday night that all I've had is black coffee and maybe half a sleeve of saltines. 

So, to say the voices or the monitoring are causing the lack of appetite? I just don't know. I haven't noticed it working like that, like, 'Oh, I heard a voice whisper my name, so now I can't eat my sandwich.' It doesn't feel like cause and effect. It's more like... I just don't have any desire for food anymore, period. It's just gone. Whether they're watching my charting times or not, the food just sits there.
Do you find that your lack of appetite is worse on days when you're feeling down or in a heavy fog?

Well, see, the thing about those days... it's not just a fog that rolls in later in the afternoon, you know? It usually starts the absolute second I open my eyes. Honestly, most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling... it's like the day is already completely ruined before I even put on my badge. 

And you know, my badge, I always keep it right on the nightstand next to my keys and my wallet so I don't forget it, because if you forget it you have to go through the main security desk and get a temporary paper badge and it's just a whole administrative ordeal that I don't want to deal with. But on those mornings, just looking at it sitting there on the wood... it's like it weighs ten pounds. Just reaching over to pick it up and clip it to my scrubs feels like climbing a mountain. That hollow feeling just sits right in the middle of my chest, and it just drains every single ounce of motivation I have before my feet even touch the floor. 

So, when you ask if the lack of appetite is worse on those days... yeah. Definitely. Because when you wake up and you already feel like everything is ruined and pointless, when you have that absolute emptiness inside you, food doesn't even register as a possibility. I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling fan, dreading having to get up, and the thought of going to the kitchen to even make a piece of toast or pour a bowl of cereal makes me feel... I don't know, just completely exhausted. I've tried explaining it to my sister before, and she always says, "just eat a little something, it'll give you energy for your shift," but she doesn't understand that when that heavy fog is there, my stomach just completely shuts down. It's like my whole system goes offline. 

So yeah, the worse that hollow feeling is in the morning, the less chance there is of me eating anything at all. I'll just drag myself up, put on the badge, and go through the motions at the clinic on an entirely empty tank. It's just... it's too much effort to chew when you feel that weighed down.
Do the voices you hear ever tell you to do something or are they mostly commenting on what you're doing?

Well, like I was saying before about the hallway and the phlebotomy room... they don't really give me orders. It's not like they're telling me, you know, "go do this," or "drop those vials," or anything like that. I've never had a voice tell me to actually perform an action. 

It's really just... well, it's exactly what I was mentioning earlier. It's those short little comments. I'll just be standing there, completely alone, and I'll hear my name. Just my name, clear as a bell, right behind my shoulder. Or that phrase, "he messed up again." That's the one that really gets me when I'm near the phlebotomy room. And it's never an instruction, it's just this running commentary, like someone is standing right there observing me and judging every little move I make. 

Like, I could be organizing the tourniquets—because we have the standard blue rubber ones and then the latex-free fabric ones, and you have to keep them in completely separate bins because if a patient has a severe latex allergy and you grab the wrong one, it's a massive liability for the clinic, so I'm always very, very careful about it—and right as I'm sorting them, making sure everything is perfect, I'll just hear it. "He messed up again." Just criticizing me. But I turn around, and like I said, there is absolutely nobody there. It's just me and the supplies.

And the thing that still confuses me, which I was trying to figure out earlier, is that it happens even on days when I'm not especially sad. You'd think it would only happen when that heavy, hollow feeling is really weighing me down, right? But no. I could be having a perfectly fine afternoon, not feeling down at all, just doing my regular inventory and actually feeling decent about the shift, and then... bam. A comment out of thin air in a totally empty room. So, yeah, to answer your question, they never tell me what to do. They just watch and comment.
Are the comments from the voices usually about your work or something else?

It's... well, it feels like it's about work, mostly, just because of the context, you know? Like I was telling you just a minute ago, it's always those same short comments, like 'he messed up again,' or just someone calling my name. And because it happens when I'm in the clinic, my brain immediately thinks it's about my job performance. 

Like, if I'm walking down that long back hallway—the one that connects the main waiting area to the biohazard disposal room, which is always freezing, by the way, because the thermostat back there has been broken since October and maintenance just refuses to put in a work order for it, no matter how many times the clinic manager emails them—I'll just be walking down that hall with a tray of vials, completely alone, and I'll hear my name. Just spoken right behind me. Or I'll be near the phlebotomy room setting up the cart and hear 'he messed up again.' And I'll stop what I'm doing, and I'll look around, and I'll even check the adjacent exam rooms, but there is absolutely nobody there. The hallway is empty, the room is empty. It's just me.

And the part that really throws me off, which I know I just mentioned, but I really want to emphasize this because it just doesn't make any logical sense to me... it can happen even on days when I'm not especially sad. I could be having a completely normal shift, getting all my inventory done on time, not feeling that horrible emptiness in my chest at all. I could actually be feeling okay! And then out of nowhere, there's that voice in an empty room, criticizing me. So, is it about work? I guess it has to be, right? Because why else would they be telling me I messed up while I'm standing there holding medical supplies? It just always seems to happen right there in the hallway or the lab area, whether I'm having a good day or a bad day.
Do the voices you hear ever change what they say or is it always the same comments?

You know, I was actually just thinking about that the other day when I was doing the inventory. It's funny you ask, because... no, they really don't change. It's honestly like a broken record. I know I sound like I'm just repeating myself here, but it really is always just those same exact short comments. It's either just my first name, called out plain as day, or it's that one specific phrase, "he messed up again." I've never heard them say anything like, I don't know, "he dropped the tubes" or "he's running late." It's always exactly "he messed up again." 

And it's so strange because it's always in those exact same spots, too. Like I've been saying, it's either out in that freezing back hallway or right there near the phlebotomy room. I'll literally stop what I'm doing and check every corner of the room. I'll even look behind the privacy screens—because we have those heavy vinyl folding privacy screens in the draw stations, and the wheels always get jammed on the ceiling tracks so you have to really yank them to close them properly, and sometimes people leave them half-open—so I'll check behind them just to be absolutely sure. But there is just nobody there. Not a single soul. Just me.

And the part that really just completely baffles me, and I know I just brought this up but it's the thing I just cannot get past, is that it doesn't even matter what kind of mood I'm in. It’s not like it only happens when I'm having one of those terrible mornings where I can't even look at my badge because I feel so hollow. I could be having a completely fine day, not feeling sad in the slightest, just going about my business and actually feeling alright, and I'll still hear it. So yeah, to answer your question, it doesn't change. It's just the same short comments, over and over, in an empty room, whether I'm feeling down or not.
Have the voices you hear ever told you to do something that you felt compelled to act on?

I know we kind of just touched on this, and I feel like I'm talking in circles a bit here, but no, absolutely not. I've never felt compelled to act on anything, mainly because... well, like I was explaining, they aren't telling me to do anything in the first place. 

It's really just those same short comments. Just my name, or that phrase, "he messed up again." That's it. There's no instruction attached to it, no command, nothing for me to even act on, you know? 

And it always happens in those same exact spots—out in that back hallway or right near the phlebotomy room. And like I've been saying, I'll be completely alone. I could be standing there, maybe organizing the butterfly needles—we use the 21-gauge green ones and the 23-gauge light blue ones, and you have to make sure the boxes are facing outward so the phlebotomists can just grab them quickly during the morning rush, because if they have to fumble around looking for the right gauge it backs up the whole waiting room—and right as I'm doing that, I'll just hear it. "He messed up again." 

So I guess the only thing I'm ever "compelled" to do is stop what I'm doing and check the room. I'll put down the boxes, turn around, look behind the chairs, but there is absolutely nobody there. The room is completely empty. If I actually made a mistake, there's a whole protocol for that with incident report forms, but I haven't done anything wrong, I'm just standing by myself.

And I know I keep bringing this up, but it's just the part that is so baffling to me... this happens even on days when I'm not especially sad. I could be having a perfectly fine shift, feeling totally okay, none of that heavy, hollow feeling dragging me down, and I'll still hear my name or that criticism out of nowhere in an empty room. So, no, I never feel compelled to do anything dangerous or act on the voices, because they just observe and criticize. They never tell me what to do.
Do the voices you hear seem to happen more often when you're feeling down or empty inside?

Well, see, this is exactly what I've been trying to explain, and I know I keep hammering on this one point, but it's just because it makes zero sense to me. You'd think they would happen more when I'm feeling empty, right? But no, not really. 

In fact, there was this period a little while back when my mood had actually eased up enough that I was getting through the day pretty well. I was even running a little again—just short jogs in the morning before my shift, you know, because I finally had the energy to actually lace up my sneakers and get out the door instead of just staring at the wall for an hour. I was feeling pretty close to normal, or at least not dragged down by that horrible heaviness. 

But even during that time, when the depression was mostly lifted and I was actually feeling decent, for several weeks I still heard those exact same comments out in the empty hallways at the clinic. It didn't stop or slow down at all. I'd be having a great morning, heart pumping, feeling fine, and then I'd get to work and hear my name or 'he messed up again' when there was absolutely no one around. 

And... well, on top of that, during that same period when my mood was better, I was also doing this thing where I kept reading the staff schedule—the big printed one they pin up on the corkboard in the breakroom, the one that shows all the shift rotations for the month—and I kept reading it over and over like it had these hidden warnings about me. I'd just stand there staring at the grid, looking at where my name was placed next to the phlebotomy block or the inventory block, completely convinced there was some secret message buried in how the hours were laid out, warning me about something bad that was going to happen. 

So even when I was feeling fine, running again, getting through my day without that hollow ache... the voices in the empty hall and that weird feeling about the schedule were still right there, just as strong as ever. So to answer your question, no, it really doesn't seem to matter if I'm feeling down or not.
Do you think the people monitoring you, as you believe, are trying to harm you or is it something else?

Harm me? Like, physically? No, I don't think they're going to jump out of the shadows and attack me or anything like that. It's not... it's not that kind of harm. It's more like professional harm, or trying to ruin my life, really. I just... I keep getting completely stuck on the idea that certain people at the clinic are watching my charting times. Because, you see, whenever we log the inventory or input the daily draw stats into the computer system, it timestamps every single keystroke. It logs exactly when you open the file and exactly when you hit submit. 

And I know I was just talking about the staff schedule a minute ago, the big printed one on the corkboard in the breakroom? Well, that ties right into this. They are leaving these little signs in the schedule to show me they’re building a case against me. It's like they're mocking me with it. I'll look at the grid, and the way my shift hours are staggered or the specific colored highlighter they use over my name—we usually use yellow, but sometimes it's pink or green—it perfectly corresponds to the exact minutes I spent charting the day before. It's like they're broadcasting that they are tracking my every move and compiling this massive file to get me fired, or to prove I'm incompetent, or... I don't even know what the end goal is, but they are definitely building a case.

I actually went and talked to my supervisor about it. I went right into her office—it's this tiny room just past the main elevators on the second floor—and I explained the whole thing. I told her about the charting times, the colored highlighters, the signs in the schedule, all of it. And she just looked at me, sighed, and told me it’s just the new workflow. She said corporate changed how the hours are blocked out and that nobody is tracking my timestamps or leaving me messages. 

But I just... I can't let it go. Even with her telling me to my face that it's just the new workflow, I keep getting stuck on it. I can't stop thinking about it. I just stand there staring at the board, knowing they are building this case against me, piece by piece, just waiting for the right moment to drop it on me. So, no, not physical harm, but they are definitely trying to take me down.
Do you think the people you believe are monitoring you are doing so because of something specific you've done or because of who you are?

Well, I guess... I think it's really just because of who I am, honestly. Because, you see, I just... I keep thinking I’m this massive burden to the clinic. And to my family, too, really. It's like I just carry this awful weight around, knowing I'm dragging everyone down, so it makes perfect sense to me that they'd want to track my every move and build a case to get rid of me. 

Because I just... I blame myself for everything. Even these tiny, small mistakes, they just eat at me. Like, for example, the room turnovers. When a patient leaves, we have to go in and wipe down the draw chairs with those purple-top CaviWipes—you have to make sure you're wearing gloves, obviously, because the chemicals are really harsh on your skin—and then we restock the gauze pads, check the biohazard bins, make sure the sharps container isn't past that little black fill line, all of that. It usually takes maybe three or four minutes if you're moving fast. 

But sometimes I'm just... a little delayed. Like last week, I was maybe five minutes late turning over Room 4 because I was getting fresh boxes of the medium gloves from the supply closet down the hall. And I just felt... I still feel like I completely harmed everyone’s whole day. Just because of that one small delay. I felt like I ruined the entire flow of the clinic, backed up the waiting room, made the phlebotomists stressed, made the patients angry... all because of me. 

And I can't stop thinking about it. I just sit there and blame myself, feeling like I've ruined everything for everyone. I'm just such a burden. So when you ask why they're monitoring me... it's because I'm me. I'm the guy who messes up the room turnover and ruins the whole shift, so of course they're watching my timestamps. They have to be. Because I'm just a liability to everyone around me.
Do you think the people monitoring you are aware of the mistakes you feel guilty about, such as the delayed room turnover?

Oh, they absolutely know. They have to know. I mean, how could they not? If they are tracking my timestamps on the computer system like I told you, they can see exactly how long I was away from the desk getting those medium gloves from the supply closet. They see that five-minute gap in the log where nothing was entered, where I was holding everyone up. 

And when I realize they see it, that's when that horrible, heavy feeling just completely crashes down on me. I get so incredibly down, like I can barely lift my arms to wipe down the next draw chair or even look the other staff in the eye because I know I'm such a massive failure and I've ruined their day.
